data.gui#gui:
go-theca/gui is a portable desktop GUI for Theca containers, built with go-widgets. Release: v0.4.0 (v0.1.0 was the first). This page is written from the README and CHANGELOG at that tag; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins.
go install github.com/go-theca/gui@latest # the binary is named gui It is pure Go (CGO_ENABLED=0): a Cocoa window on macOS, X11 or Wayland on Linux, Win32 on Windows.
data.limits#Limits: Share needs an exFAT volume. Since v0.2.0, Create offers the filesystem: exFAT (the default, laid through the container by share.Format of theca v0.4.0, as theca create --fs exfat does; a volume too small for exFAT is refused and the half-made file removed) or a raw volume. A raw one cannot be shared. A shareable container is made from the GUI. Mounting is measured on macOS. Linux (gvfs) and Windows (MSFT_SmbMapping) go through the same library but have not been run from this GUI. FIDO2 is measured on a real key on macOS only; on Linux and Windows it is built but not measured. The Linux and Windows windows are built and cross-compiled in CI, but have not been run by hand yet. There is no file picker yet: paths are typed or pasted. No rollback counter support.
data.v030#Since v0.3.0: Share on the network, a toggle beside Share: it serves on every interface with message signing and encryption required of every client (theca share.Options{Network: true}). A warning says that anyone on the network with the password can connect. The screen shows where it listens and the port; the password stays hidden until Show password and is cleared at stop, lock and close. Live-tested on macOS: smbutil reports encryption and signing required. Keyslots screen, from the Container screen: it shows the recorded slots and which ones the password and/or recovery code you type now open, and removes the slot of a factor set while a different set to keep must still open the container. A removal that would leave no way in is refused and changes nothing. A removal only stops access to this copy. The security key’s state is shown on screen: “touch your key”, or “type its PIN” (masked, emptied on Submit, never in a message), then touch again. On Windows the screen says that Windows shows its own dialog. These states are tested with a fake key; a real-key run has been done by hand on macOS only. It uses theca v0.8.0 (FIDO2 on Linux and Windows). v0.3.1 used theca v0.10.2 and v0.4.0 uses theca v0.23.0. v0.3.1’s theca v0.10.2 fixes a second mount failing on macOS (“authentication error (errno 80)”): every share now has its own random account name. Live tests: network share 6 of 6, local share 3 of 3 (the failure was intermittent before).
data.v040#Since v0.4.0: My profiles, from Home: lists the profiles of containers.toml (the file theca profile add writes) with their state (closed; open with the mount point and since when; or the error), and opens and closes them as theca open NAME and theca close NAME do. Open starts the same background process through session.Start of theca v0.23.0. The password, recovery code and PIN come from the references in the profile (keychain, Secret Service, KeePassXC): the screen never asks for or holds a secret. While the process waits for the security key the row says “touch your security key now” and the key hint is shown; Cancel ends the wait. The GUI needs the theca command: it looks on the PATH, then in ~/.local/bin, ~/go/bin, /usr/local/bin and /opt/homebrew/bin, and says how to install it when it finds none. The profile stays open when the window is closed, as after theca open. Tested with fakes and against a real session socket; the app was started once on macOS against a temporary containers.toml, and no real container was opened from this screen.
data.what#What it does:
It does what the theca command does, in a window: create a container, unlock it, look at it, verify it, copy a file in and out, pair a FIDO2 security key with it, and share the exFAT filesystem inside it.
Create. File, size, filesystem (exFAT, the default, or a raw volume), policy (any or 2of3) and the password twice. The recovery code is shown once, and the screen cannot be left until you tick I have written it down. Unlock. Password and/or recovery code, and a Use security key toggle. Container. Size, key slots, journal, rollback status; Verify, Import, Export (to a new file), Enroll security key, Close container. Share / Stop sharing. On the Container screen, Share serves the exFAT filesystem inside the container over SMB on a loopback address and mounts it in the file manager with no password dialog, through the share package of theca v0.3.0. The screen shows where it is shared and mounted, and Open in file manager shows the volume. The share stops, unmounting first, on the toggle, on Close container and on closing the window: always before the container is committed and closed. The share’s account password is never shown. A container with no exFAT inside is refused with a message.

data.commands#What each command does: create --fs exfat formats the volume through the container itself (go-filesystems/exfat FormatImage). No decrypted copy is ever written to disk. serve unlocks the container and serves its exFAT over SMB (2.1 to 3.1.1, signed) using go-filesystems/smb v0.15.0. serve --mount mounts the share in the file manager (Finder, GNOME Files, Explorer) with no password dialog, through go-fileshare/automount: the password goes to the operating system’s mount service as a value. At stop it unmounts first, so the client flushes through the server, then commits and closes the container. --credentials-out is no longer required when --mount is given. --credentials-out writes the URL, user and password to a file (mode 0600, created only if absent, removed at exit), for another client. One of --mount and --credentials-out is required. Writes are committed to the container every --sync (default 5 s) and when the server stops.
data.journal-resize#Resizing the journal of a:
Since v0.27.0, theca journal resize FILE --out NEW [--entries N] writes a copy of FILE with another journal size (by default the size theca create would pick). The size fixes the layout, so FILE is never rewritten. NEW keeps every key slot, the policy, the counter binding and the content; it is created exclusively, synced, reopened and compared with FILE by the hash of the volume before anything is reported. FILE is opened with your usual factors (--password-from, --device). The command does not swap the files: it prints the two mv commands. Mount the copy once before deleting the old file: with a rollback counter, that mount moves the counter past FILE, which is then refused. Until then FILE still opens. The speed gain on a resized container has not been measured yet (the machine was under load).
theca journal resize vault.theca --out vault-new.theca --password-from keychain:theca/vault --device bio
data.limit#A limit: A copy of a file written through the share is one transaction per journal budget, not one per file (DESIGN section 19, I12). A crash in the middle of a large copy can leave the exFAT metadata of that copy half-written, as on a disk.
data.measured#Measured, and where:
Measured on macOS 27 only (2026-11-16): --mount lands in /Volumes/theca over SMB 3.1.1 signed with AES-128-GMAC, a file written through it survives a stop and a remount, and verify passes. Linux (GNOME Files, through gvfs) and Windows (Explorer, a drive letter through MSFT_SmbMapping) use the same command; neither has been measured with theca yet.
--network was also measured on macOS: smbutil reports AES-128-GCM, GMAC, and ENCRYPTION_REQUIRED and SIGNING_REQUIRED both TRUE.
data.security#Security: Two modes. The data served is decrypted, so serve has two modes: Loopback (the default). serve listens on a loopback address only. A non-loopback --addr is refused, and the refusal names --network. --network (share.Options{Network: true}, since theca v0.5.0). serve listens beyond loopback only with message signing and encryption required together (of every session and of the share), never one without the other: a client that cannot do both (SMB 2.1, or one that refuses encryption) is refused. This is go-filesystems/smb v0.15.0 RequireSigning, EncryptData and RequireEncryption. A warning goes to standard error. It does not make serving safe on a hostile network: anyone who can reach the address and has the password can read and write the container’s files, and the password is in --credentials-out. With --network --mount and an unspecified address (0.0.0.0, ::), the local mount uses 127.0.0.1 on the same port; another machine uses this machine’s address with that port. The GUI has no network option: it always serves loopback. One random account per share, never printed or passed as an argument. Since v0.10.2 the account name is random too: theca- and 8 random base32 characters (Share.User(), share.UserPrefix), written in --credentials-out. Before, every share used the name theca, and on macOS a second mount in the same session failed (“authentication error (errno 80)”), because macOS replays a stale credential for a fixed account name on 127.0.0.1. A fixed name failed 12 of 12 repeats; a random name 0 of 120 (the smb author’s harness).
data.serve#Serving the files inside:
Since v0.2.0, Theca can hold an exFAT filesystem and serve it over SMB, so a container is used like a disk without ever writing a decrypted copy. This page is written from the README at tag v0.2.0 (section “Serving the files inside”) and its CHANGELOG; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins.
theca create vault.theca --size 4G --fs exfat # a container holding an exFAT filesystem theca serve vault.theca --mount # appears in the Finder; Ctrl-C unmounts and stops # serving smb://127.0.0.1:58738/theca; Ctrl-C to stop # mounted at /Volumes/theca theca serve vault.theca --credentials-out creds.json # or: hand the account to another client
data.write-speed#Write speed: The journal budget is also the batch: every commit costs about four flushes (F_FULLFSYNC on macOS) whatever its size. Since v0.26.1, theca create sizes the journal at one entry per 16 sectors, from 64 to 4096 (--journal overrides). Measured on macOS, single core, 64 MiB written in a row: 12.0 to 92.4 MiB/s through the library, and 7.6 to 28.8 MiB/s through the share (32 KiB SMB writes, --sync 5 s). The size is fixed at creation: a container made before v0.26.1 keeps its 64 entries. Linux is not measured.

data.api#API: share.Start(ctx, c, Options{Addr, Name, Sync, Mount}) serves the exFAT inside an unlocked container over SMB on loopback and optionally mounts it. URL, User, Password and MountPath describe the share. Password exists to hand the account to another client; it is a secret, never to be shown or logged. Done and Err: a failed commit or server ends the share, and Err says why. Stop is idempotent: it unmounts, closes the server and closes the filesystem. It never closes the container; the caller does, after Stop. A container with no exFAT inside is refused with share.ErrNoFilesystem. Breaking in v0.10.2 (below v1): the share.User constant is gone. The account name is random per share: use Share.User() (the prefix is share.UserPrefix, then 8 random base32 characters). Only a loopback address is served, unless Options.Network is true (theca v0.5.0): then a non-loopback address is served with signing and encryption both required. Share.Addr() returns the address served. Breaking in v0.5.0 (below v1): share.CheckAddr(addr string, network bool) takes the network switch; without it a non-loopback address is refused. Since v0.4.0, share.Format(c) makes a fresh container shareable: it lays the exFAT filesystem onto the container’s volume, through the container. theca create --fs exfat uses it, and so can any front end that creates containers (the GUI’s Create does). A volume too small is refused. theca serve is a thin front over this package. Its behaviour is unchanged, except that the address error now reads address X: only a loopback address is served and a failed mount no longer prints the serving line first.
data.share#The share package:
Since v0.3.0 (v0.4.0 for Format, v0.5.0 for Network), the logic of theca serve is a library package, github.com/go-theca/theca/share, so that a program other than the command line (the GUI imports it) can share a container. This page is written from the README at tag v0.5.0 (section “Sharing the files inside”) and its CHANGELOG; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins.
s, err := share.Start(ctx, c, share.Options{ Addr: "127.0.0.1:0", Name: "theca", Sync: 5 * time.Second, Mount: true, }) if err != nil { // share.ErrNoFilesystem: no exFAT inside return err } fmt.Println(s.URL(), s.MountPath()) // smb://127.0.0.1:58738/theca /Volumes/theca // <-s.Done() fires when a commit or the server fails; s.Err() says why. err = s.Stop() // unmount, close the server, close the filesystem (idempotent) c.Close() // the caller closes the container, after Stop

data.cli#Command line:
go install github.com/go-theca/theca/cmd/theca@latest theca create vault.theca --size 1G # asks the password twice, prints the recovery code once theca info vault.theca # unlock and describe theca verify vault.theca # authenticate every sector and tree node theca import vault.theca --password-from keychain:theca/vault --offset 0 < disk.img theca export vault.theca --password-from keychain:theca/vault > disk.img theca enroll-key vault.theca --recovery-from keychain:theca/rc # pair the key with the password and the recovery code theca info vault.theca --fido2 # password + key theca info vault.theca --recovery-from keychain:theca/rc --fido2 # recovery code + key Secrets never go in arguments or environment variables. The password is read from the terminal with echo off, or from a secret manager (next item).
Secret files are deprecated (v0.21.0). --password-file, --recovery-file, --pin-file, --tpm-auth-file and --tpm-owner-auth-file still work (a regular file, mode 0600 or stricter) but are hidden from the help, and each use prints a warning on standard error naming the --X-from replacement. So does a file: reference in --password-from, --recovery-from and --pin-from. --tpm-auth-from refuses file:, like the other TPM flags. A plaintext file beside a container protected by hardware keys defeats them.
Secrets from a reference (v0.12.0). --password-from, --recovery-from and --pin-from take a reference instead of a plaintext file, as go-authn/secretsource defines it: keychain:SERVICE/ACCOUNT (macOS Keychain), secretservice:SERVICE/ACCOUNT or secretservice:KEY=VALUE[,KEY=VALUE] (GNOME Keyring, KWallet, KeePassXC’s Secret Service integration on Linux), and since v0.14.0 keepassxc:URL (the only form since v0.15.0), the entry whose URL field is that URL (KeePassXC’s browser-integration protocol, macOS and Linux; fill the entry’s URL field, for example https://theca.invalid/vault). keepassxc:by-uuid/... and keepassxc:by-path/... are refused: KeePassXC 2.8.0 crashes on an entry without a URL. No scheme runs a command. The -file flags are unchanged and exclusive with the -from flags. KeePassXC needs Browser Integration enabled and one secretsource keepassxc associate; secretsource check REF verifies a reference without printing the secret.
theca info vault.theca --password-from keychain:theca/vault theca info vault.theca --password-from 'keepassxc:https://theca.invalid/vault' --fido2 --pin-from 'keepassxc:https://fido.invalid/yubikey-5c' Storing the new secrets (v0.16.0). theca create --password-to REF [--generate N] [--recovery-to REF] [--replace] puts the new password and the recovery code straight into a secret manager (keychain:, secretservice:, keepassxc:URL, through secretsource store), so neither is typed into a file or left on the terminal. --generate N draws the password (letters and digits) and needs --password-to; --password-to and --generate exclude --password-file and --password-from. The password is stored before the container is created, so a failed store creates nothing. The recovery code is stored after creation; if that store fails it is printed after all (the only copy) and create exits with the error.
create prints the recovery code once, on standard output. If you redirect it to a file, that file gets your umask (often 0644): restrict it, or better, write the code down on paper.
import reads its data from standard input, so it needs --password-file or --recovery-file. It is not one atomic transaction: on an error, the bytes written before the error are kept.
enroll-key makes one discoverable credential on the key (relying party theca, credProtect 3, hmac-secret) and pairs it with the password, and with the recovery code too when --recovery-file names it. The key is touched twice: to register, then to confirm.
Pairing only adds a way in (v0.17.0). Under policy any the password alone (and the recovery code alone) still open the container after enroll-key. It says which still do and prints the command that removes the password-only slot. enroll-key --require does it in one run: after pairing, the key is touched once more to prove the password with the key opens the container, and only then is the password-only slot removed (nothing is removed if the proof fails; the pairing stays). It does not remove the recovery-only slot: that code is the way in if the key is lost, so under policy any it still opens the container alone until you run theca slots remove --remove recovery --keep password+fido2 (after which a lost key means a lost container). A recovery code that was not presented cannot be tested, and the output says so.
--fido2 adds the attached key to an unlock. Since v0.10.3 the key’s built-in verification (fingerprint) is used only when its GetInfo says uv is true (CTAP 2.1 6.4). On CTAP2_ERR_UV_INVALID the tries left are read and shown, and the attempt is retried up to 5 times. On UV_BLOCKED, no tries left, or no fingerprint enrolled (NOT_ALLOWED), theca says so and uses the PIN when one is set, else fails with ErrUVLocked. This is not measured on a real YubiKey Bio. A key without a fingerprint asks for its PIN, read from --pin-file (mode 0600 or stricter) or from the terminal, never from an argument.
theca create --fs exfat and theca serve (with --mount) are described in Serving and mounting.
data.counter#Rollback counter (v0.9.0 to v0.1: theca create vault.theca --size 1G --counter tpm # defines an NV counter, binds the container to it theca info vault.theca --counter tpm # rollback protected: true (TPM NV counter ...) theca info vault.theca --counter tpm --accept-rollback # accept an older copy on purpose (loud); needs the counter theca counter rebind vault.theca --counter tpm --tpm-owner-auth-file owner # the counter is gone: bind to a new one --counter tpm defines a TPM 2.0 NV counter (go-tpm2/tpm2 v0.9.0) and binds the container to it. The counter advances once per mount, not per commit: an older copy of the container is refused with ErrRollback before anything is written. The copy taken during the current session is the window that stays open (DESIGN section 5.4). Every command that opens the container needs --counter tpm again (and --tpm-auth-file if you set one), and opens the file read-write, because a mount rebinds the header. A protected container opened without the flag is refused with a message naming it. Without --counter tpm, a container is not protected: an older copy would be accepted. --tpm-device is a device path, or unix:SOCKET for a software TPM. The default is /dev/tpmrm0 on Linux and tbs: (TPM Base Services, through go-tpm2/devtpm’s OpenTBS) on Windows since v0.26.0. macOS has no TPM and says so unless a device is named. Windows is not measured on a real TPM: on a Windows 11 VM without a TPM the real tbs.dll answers TBS_E_TPM_NOT_FOUND, and no counter has been run there. When the counter is gone (the owner undefined the index, or TPM2_Clear, a BIOS reset or a reinstall removed it; the index has no POLICY_DELETE, which would need platform authorization), the container cannot be opened. The message says so and names the recovery, theca counter rebind FILE --counter tpm --tpm-owner-auth-file F (v0.10.0). Earlier text, including this page’s, said --accept-rollback would help; it does not, because it needs a counter that exists and is ahead of the container. rebind needs the factors that open the container and the TPM owner password. It defines a counter (at the recorded handle if free, else the first free one), binds the header to it and increments it. Since v0.10.1 a still-present old counter is deleted first: otherwise a copy made just before the rebind would still open with it. Rollback protection then restarts from that moment; nothing is checked against the old counter. An old copy of the container shows the same refusal as a reset TPM: do not rebind to open one. New counters carry TPMA_NV_NO_DA (go-tpm2/tpm2 v0.10.0), so a wrong authValue file does not count towards the TPM’s lockout. Counters made by v0.9.0 are still opened. The TPM is pinned (v0.18.0, go-theca/theca#39). create and counter rebind record in the authenticated header the identity of the TPM the counter is on: the digest of the Name of its endorsement key (the ECC P-256 EK template of the TCG EK Credential Profile, created transiently and flushed, never persistent; go-tpm2/tpm2 v0.11.0). Every mount compares it before reading the counter; a counter on another TPM is refused, naming both identities (first 6 bytes in hex) and the recovery. info shows counter TPM identity: . It needs the endorsement authValue to be empty (the default). Containers made before v0.18.0 carry no identity: they open as before, with a warning at every mount, until theca counter rebind pins them (it replaces the counter, so protection restarts from that moment). Threat model, by attacker. Someone who replaces the container file with an older copy: stopped, as before. Someone who brings another TPM (a fresh software TPM, a replaced TPM) and defines the same index on it at the old bound: stopped since v0.18.0, not in a container made earlier and not rebound. Someone who controls the TPM in use (the host of a virtual TPM, a program standing between theca and the TPM): not stopped; the identity names a TPM, it does not prove the TPM answering is that one, because the EK public is not secret. Someone who holds a copy of the TPM’s state (a software TPM’s state directory, a VM snapshot) holds its endorsement seed: not stopped, and the counter rolls back with the state. A bus interposer forging the answers of a discrete TPM: not stopped. TPM2_NV_Certify under an attestation key would authenticate the answers; it was weighed and deferred (DESIGN section 5.4.1), because it does not change the outcome against the other attackers. Measured against a user-space software TPM (swtpm) on a Linux machine, not a hardware TPM. The counter has not been run against a hardware TPM.
data.daily#Daily use: profiles, open, close (:
A long command line is the price of several factors. A profile names a container once; theca open then uses the password from the secret manager and one touch of the key, with nothing new stored anywhere:
# once: references only, nothing secret is written, nothing secret is read theca profile add vault ~/vault/vault.theca \ --password-from 'keepassxc:https://theca.invalid/vault' --device bio # every day theca open vault # manager + one touch; mounts; frees the terminal theca status # what is open, where it is mounted theca close vault # unmounts, commits, closes The profile file is containers.toml in os.UserConfigDir()/theca, mode 0600 in a 0700 directory; a file another user can read is refused. It holds the container’s path, password-from, recovery-from and pin-from (keychain:, secretservice:, keepassxc:; file: is refused), device, counter, tpm-device, tpm-auth-from, tpm-endorsement-auth-from, share, sync and close-on-lock. theca profile add checks the syntax of the references and never reads a secret; profile list and profile remove NAME list and delete (the container and the manager’s entries stay). A counter whose authValue is derived from the master key needs no tpm-auth-from; counter = "tpm" stays in the profile, because the header can be read only after the unlock. open starts a background process that holds the unlocked container, serves it on a loopback address and mounts it in the file manager, then returns. The process locks the container file first, so a second open of the same container is refused before any unlock or counter increment. close and status talk to that process over a Unix socket, mode 0600 in a 0700 directory ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/theca, else os.UserConfigDir()/theca/run), which refuses any user but the owner (SO_PEERCRED, LOCAL_PEERCRED). A message is one JSON line of at most 4096 bytes, with no unknown field; no secret crosses it. The profile parser and the socket decoder are fuzzed. session.Start (v0.23.0) is what open does to start that process, as a library call: session.Start(ctx, exe, name, notice) runs exe _serve NAME with no terminal (standard input is /dev/null), waits until the container is unlocked and mounted, hands each line the process writes to its standard error while it unlocks (the security key’s touch notice) to notice, and returns the session.Info. A cancelled ctx kills the process. session.StartAttached is the terminal form theca open uses. The gui uses it for its profiles screen. Auto-close (close-on-lock, default true). On Linux theca asks logind over D-Bus: Session.Lock, LockedHint, PrepareForSleep, PrepareForShutdown. On macOS (v0.22.0) it listens for com.apple.screenIsLocked, NSWorkspaceWillSleepNotification and NSWorkspaceSessionDidResignActiveNotification: no polling lag, and the container is closed before the machine sleeps. The observers are proven at start with a notification of the process’s own name; if they cannot be registered or heard, theca falls back to reading CGSSessionScreenIsLocked every two seconds (a wall-clock jump the monotonic clock did not make counts as a sleep), and theca open prints which mode is active. The container is then unmounted, committed and closed. Windows has no source yet: the container stays open until theca close. Not measured against a real lock or sleep on either system: the signals are tested with fakes, and on macOS with a real round trip of a notification of our own name.
data.factors#Factors:
A container is opened by one of three factors:
a password, stretched with Argon2id; a recovery code, printed once by create and never stored; a FIDO2 security key, which is never a factor alone: it always pairs with the password or with the recovery code. The policy is chosen at creation. --policy any (the default) lets the password alone, or the recovery code alone, open the container. --policy 2of3 needs two of the three: password and recovery code from the start, and a FIDO2 key (enroll-key) then pairs with each.
data.fido2-os#FIDO2 on each OS:
From the README at v0.9.0:
OS Route PIN and prompts Status macOS CTAP over IOKit HID (go-macos/fido) theca asks: --pin-file or the terminal measured on a YubiKey 5, firmware 5.7.4 Linux CTAP over /dev/hidraw* (go-gnulinux/fido), pure Go theca asks, as on macOS fakes and a kernel-made HID device only; not measured on a real key Windows webauthn.dll (go-mswin/webauthn) Windows asks: a Windows Security dialog collects the PIN or fingerprint, so --pin-file does not apply fakes and struct layouts only; not measured on a real key On Linux /dev/hidraw* belongs to root on a stock system: install a udev rule giving your user access to FIDO keys (libfido2’s 70-u2f.rules); theca then says “a security key is attached but this user cannot open it” instead of “no key”. On Windows, hmac-secret needs WebAuthn API version 6 (Windows 11 reports 9), and when several Theca credentials are on the key, Windows has the person pick one.
data.later#Later releases:
v0.6.1: go-filesystems/smb v0.16.1, with per-source connection caps (32 per source, 16 pre-auth; loopback is not exempt, and the limit is far above one Finder client) and a zone-id fix.
v0.7.0: AES-256-CTR runs through go-encryptions/ctr (round keys expanded once, one kernel call per sector, no allocation; Zeroize wipes the round keys), and Argon2id through go-encryptions/argon2, the x/crypto/argon2 code with a NEON kernel on arm64. See the performance section below.
v0.8.0: FIDO2 on Linux (go-gnulinux/fido v0.5.1, CTAP over hidraw) and on Windows (go-mswin/webauthn v0.5.0, webauthn.dll). The transport is chosen by GOOS. See “FIDO2 on each OS” below.
v0.9.0: a TPM rollback counter. See “Rollback counter” below.
v0.10.2: the share’s account name is random (theca- and 8 random base32 characters), which fixes a second mount failing on macOS. See Serving and mounting.
v0.24.0 (security, go-theca/theca#66): a counter that is asked for is required. A container whose header names no counter (made without one, or a copy from before counter rebind) is refused under --counter tpm with “this container has no rollback counter, but –counter tpm was asked: an older copy may have been restored”; theca.Open returns ErrCounterRequired when given a counter. close-on-lock fails closed: if the lock watcher cannot start, open fails, and --close-on-lock=false is the explicit opt-out. On Linux only logind’s signals about this process’s own session count, and a session already locked at start closes at once; a screen locker that tells logind nothing (bare i3lock, swaylock) is not seen. The loopback SMB share requires message signing. profile add refuses a line Parse would refuse.
v0.25.0 (security, go-theca/theca#68): the key material in memory.
The FIDO2 PIN and the recovery code are []byte, wiped after use like the password (Unlock.Recovery, RecoveryFactor, format.ParseRecoveryCode and the fido2 PIN callbacks changed type: a break for library callers). Two copies remain as an immutable string: the PIN at go-authn/fido’s PINToken, and the recovery code create prints. theca _serve (the detached daemon) turns core dumps off and refuses debuggers before any key exists: on Linux RLIMIT_CORE 0 and PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0, on macOS RLIMIT_CORE 0 and PT_DENY_ATTACH, nothing elsewhere. A refusal is a warning on stderr, not a stop. The master secret, the slot wrap keys and their cipher caches are locked in RAM (mlock). --mlock=auto (the default) warns once if the system refuses, --mlock=required makes a refusal an error, --mlock=off turns it off; open hands its choice to the daemon. Not locked: the AES round keys inside the CTR library, transient key-encryption keys on the stack, and the crypto/hmac pads. Cost, single core, 15 interleaved rounds, macOS arm64: open 187 us (off) against 202 us (auto) with a test-size KDF; writing 2 MiB 3.14 s against 3.21 s; reading 8 MiB 3.06 ms against 2.96 ms. The load was slightly above 8, so read the ratios. v0.10.3: FIDO2 fingerprint handling and the PIN fallback, with the new ErrUVLocked. See --fido2 above.
v0.10.0 and v0.10.1: theca counter rebind, NO_DA on new counters, the threat-model note, and a correction of v0.9.0’s recovery advice. See “Rollback counter” below.
v0.18.0: the rollback counter is pinned to the TPM it was made on; a counter on another TPM is refused. See “Rollback counter” below.
v0.20.0: theca profile, open, close and status: one command and one touch, closing on lock. See “Daily use” above.
data.performance#Performance:
Theca is measured against C references on one core with go-scikit/refbench: libsodium for XChaCha20 and Argon2id, OpenSSL for AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA-256. The procedure and the cases are in bench/README.md. Ratio is Go time divided by reference time; below 1 is faster. Both runs are on commit 6d515c5 with go1.27.4, libsodium 1.0.22 and OpenSSL 4.0.2, from 2026-11-15. Medians in ns/call; the full tables, with quartiles and allocation counts, are docs/perf-table.md and docs/perf-zen4-table.md.
case Apple M4 Max (Go / ref, ratio) AMD Zen 4 (Go / ref, ratio) Sector/XChaCha20 2286 / 4143, 0.55 faster 4016 / 9195, 0.44 faster (see caveat) Sector/AES-256-CTR 459.4 / 308.9, 1.49 slower 432.7 / 357.1, 1.21 slower Sector/Tag (HMAC-SHA-256) 1493 / 1428, 1.05 slower 1691 / 1736, 0.97 faster Sector/Seal 4290 / 5935, 0.72 faster 6140 / 11330, 0.54 faster Sector/Open 4296 / 5992, 0.72 faster 6154 / 11380, 0.54 faster Argon2id t3-m64MiB-p1 9.424e+07 / 6.306e+07, 1.49 slower 6.616e+07 / 2.662e+08, 0.25 faster (see caveat) The Apple M4 Max run was at a 1-minute load of 7.22 to 7.59 (gate 8.00); the Zen 4 machine is an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X pinned to one CPU, at a load of 0.16 to 0.35. Both runs are marked valid. A gap in a row includes Theca’s own per-sector setup cost, which is a cost of the design and not of the language.
Since v0.7.0 (the table above is the v0.1.0 run), per the CHANGELOG: Argon2id on the Apple M4 Max went from 1.54 to 0.73 of libsodium, and AES-256-CTR is 1.03x and the sector tag 1.04x OpenSSL there (#8 and #9 stay open). On Zen 4 (the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, v0.7.0): AES-256-CTR is 0.97 of OpenSSL, the sector tag 0.98, and Argon2id 0.25 of libsodium. On amd64 the Argon2id code is x/crypto’s unchanged, and libsodium’s 265 ms there was confirmed by a C control program on the same core, so that row stands as a measurement of libsodium on this machine. The control is recorded in the bench README on main: a C program calling crypto_pwhash (Argon2id, t=3, m=64 MiB, one lane) pinned to the same core gives 265 ms with the registry build and 265 to 271 ms with the legacy pkgx build of libsodium 1.0.22 (2026-11-17). The Zen 4 table is docs/perf-zen4-table.md (refbench, commit 20299a8 = v0.7.0, 1-minute load 0.31 to 0.47, OpenSSL 4.0.2): AES-256-CTR 0.97 of OpenSSL, sector tag 0.98, XChaCha20 0.44 and Argon2id 0.25 of libsodium, Seal and Open 0.53. The M4 Max table is docs/perf-table.md. The XChaCha20 row has no libsodium control yet. The M4 Max tables are in docs/perf-table.md at that tag.
Rows of the v0.1.0 run that were slower, each tracked as an issue (the changelog says #8 and #9 stay open after v0.7.0, and #10 is the Argon2id one):
#8: Sector/AES-256-CTR is slower than OpenSSL. #9: Sector/Tag (HMAC-SHA-256) is slower than OpenSSL. #10: Argon2id is slower than libsodium on arm64 (no NEON kernel in x/crypto/argon2). Caveat on the Zen 4 libsodium rows. On that machine libsodium’s XChaCha20 and Argon2id run far below their usual AVX2 speed (about 440 MB/s, and 4 times slower than Go’s Argon2id). The registry’s libsodium may be built without its SIMD code. Until a control with another libsodium build settles this, the “faster” verdicts in those two rows are not claims.
Source: https://github.com/go-theca/theca.
data.security#Security notes:
The threat model is DESIGN section 1. The places where the code differs from, or fixes the details of, the design are in its section 19, the implementation log; the FIDO2 design and its trade-offs are in HARDWARE-KEYS.md section 9, “H2 revised”.
Known limits, as the repository states them:
Rollback protection is opt-in. Every command that opens a container says whether it is protected against rollback. Without --counter tpm it is not, and an older copy would be accepted. With it, protection needs a TPM 2.0 (Linux only for now), and the TPM’s owner can delete the counter (a denial of service, not a rollback; theca counter rebind recovers, and protection restarts). FIDO2 was measured on a real key on macOS only (a YubiKey 5, firmware 5.7.4). The Linux and Windows routes exist but are not measured on a real key. A reader of the FIDO2 salt can test password guesses. The salt that a key is asked for is derived from the partner factor, so for whoever reads it (a forged authenticator, a leaked log) it is a password verifier, at Argon2id cost per guess. The salts are wiped after each call and never logged (DESIGN section 19, I21). Revoked factors: older copies of a container still open with a factor that was removed (DESIGN section 19, I15). Tree area: a container at rest is indistinguishable from random except the Merkle tree area, which shows how sparse the container is (DESIGN section 19, I11).
data.slots#Slots and caches (v0.6.0): theca slots list and theca slots remove list the key slots and remove one by the factors that open it (go-theca/theca#5). In the library: Container.RemoveFactors(remove, keep), SlotsOf, Slots and ErrLastWay. A removal that would leave the keep set with no other slot is refused before any write. Since v0.17.0 --remove and --keep also take the key: password+fido2 and recovery+fido2 (any order; a key opens a slot only with one partner). A set with the key touches it once, and the slot it opens must exist and must not be among the removed ones, so a key that is not the one enrolled here, or that holds no Theca credential, is refused before any write. To make the key mandatory: theca slots remove vault.theca --password-file pw --remove password --keep password+fido2. A container only the key opens also needs --fido2 to be opened (a second touch). Library: Container.RemoveFactorSets(remove, keep [][]Factor) and KeyPairs. The metadata block cache and the Merkle node cache of an open container are bounded (#6): OpenOptions.CacheBytes and CreateOptions.CacheBytes, default 64 MiB. Clean entries are evicted least-recently-used and wiped; dirty ones are pinned until commit; an evicted entry is authenticated again when read. Close wipes the caches.
data.theca#theca:
Theca is an encrypted container format in pure Go, with a library and a command line. The library gives an io.ReaderAt and io.WriterAt over the logical volume, and the command line creates, inspects, verifies, imports and exports containers. Since v0.2.0 it also serves the files inside over SMB and mounts them: see Serving and mounting.
The same logic is a library package, share, since v0.3.0: see Library: share.
Release: v0.25.0 (tag v0.25.0 of go-theca/theca; install with go install github.com/go-theca/theca/cmd/theca@v0.25.0). What changed is in the CHANGELOG at v0.25.0. The format may still change before v1. This page was written from v0.10.3 and the security changes of v0.24.0 and v0.25.0 are added below; where it differs from the repository, the repository wins. Its links to the repository’s design documents still point at tag v0.1.0, and the performance tables below were measured on the v0.1.0 commit.
data.what#What it is:
From the README:
authenticated sectors: XChaCha20 xor AES-256-CTR, with HMAC-SHA-256; a Merkle tree over the sector tags, and a write-ahead journal; no magic bytes; keyslots opened by a password (Argon2id), a recovery code, or both; an optional hardware rollback counter. The design, its threat model, the sources it rests on and the decisions taken are in docs/DESIGN.md; section 0 is a one-table summary.
